courseSubtitle: What to do in the first two days of an eviction case.
courseBlurb: The clock is the case. Learn to find the date that starts the timeline, read the notice and summons, and walk into the first appearance ready.

topics.title: When the clock starts
topics.description: Find the date that starts the court timeline.
topics.standfirst: The first defense move is not the argument. It is finding the date that makes every later deadline honest.
topics.scenario: A client brings in a notice to quit, a summons, and a screenshot from the landlord. Three dates appear in three different places. Only one of them starts the court timeline.
topics.rule:
**Notice — receipt date.** The notice period usually runs from when the tenant receives the notice, not when the landlord prints it.

**Summons — service date.** The answer date depends on proper service of the summons and complaint.

**Court — entry date.** Check the docket — a late or early entry can create a procedural defense.

tryIt.question: A 14-day notice is dated May 1, mailed May 2, and received by the tenant May 6. Which date do you use first?

options.text: May 1, because it is printed on the notice.
May 2, because mailing started the landlord's action.
May 6, because that is when the tenant received it.

tryIt.answer: Use May 6 — the notice period runs from receipt, not the date printed on the notice or the day it was mailed.
